title: A Great Light and a Child Is Born
summary: The gloom that closed chapter 8 gives way to light: the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, humbled in the past, will be honored, and the people walking in darkness see a great light. The oppressor's yoke is broken because a child is born, a son given, who will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace, and will reign on David's throne forever. Then the chapter turns to the northern kingdom's pride and describes three waves of judgment, each ending with the refrain that God's anger is not turned away.
story:
Chapter 8 ended with the people driven into darkness after rejecting God's word in the Assyrian crisis: they consult mediums instead of God, and they look to the earth and see only distress and anguish. Chapter 9 answers that darkness with the most famous royal promise in Isaiah. Ahaz, the king of chapter 7, had failed the test of faith; here God promises a king from David's line who will be everything Ahaz was not, carrying the government on his own shoulders instead of hiring an empire to carry it for him. The Immanuel sign of 7:14 grows into this portrait of a child with divine titles, and chapter 11 will complete it with the shoot from Jesse's stump.

The second half of the chapter (verses 8 to 21) returns to the present and begins a poem against Israel, the northern kingdom, whose refrain first appeared in 5:25 and continues to 10:4. Promise and judgment stand side by side, as they do throughout Isaiah's opening chapters. The placement is deliberate: the child whose reign rests on justice and righteousness is set beside a kingdom whose leaders mislead the people and whose society devours itself. The contrast shows what kind of king Israel needs and why no king of its own making could be that king.
historical:
Zebulun and Naphtali were tribal territories in Galilee, the northern part of Israel west and southwest of the Sea of Galilee. They were the first parts of the kingdom to fall to Assyria. In his campaigns of 733 and 732 BC Tiglath-pileser III annexed the north and organized it into Assyrian provinces named after their capitals: Duru (Dor, on the coast, the Way of the Sea), Magiddu (Megiddo, governing Galilee), and Galaza (Gilead, the land beyond the Jordan). The three names in verse 1 correspond closely to those three districts. Second Kings 15:29 lists Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali among the places Tiglath-pileser took, and records that he deported their people to Assyria. Tiglath-pileser's own summary inscriptions boast of these conquests and deportations. Archaeological surveys of Galilee show a sharp fall in settlement after the Assyrian conquest. The first land to go dark is promised the first light.

The day of Midian (verse 4) recalls Gideon's victory over the Midianites (Judges 7), when God reduced Gideon's army to three hundred so that Israel could not boast that its own hand had saved it; Isaiah returns to the same battle in 10:26. Verses 8 to 21 address the northern kingdom in its last years before the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. Its people answered early losses with defiant confidence (verse 10). Its politics were violent: four of its last six kings were assassinated. Zechariah was killed by Shallum, Shallum by Menahem, Menahem's son Pekahiah by Pekah, who struck with fifty men of Gilead, and Pekah by Hoshea (2 Kings 15:8-30). The northern tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim, sons of Joseph and brothers by descent, are pictured in verse 21 devouring each other, a fair description of those coups, and then joining together against Judah, as Pekah did with Rezin in the war of chapter 7.

Aram and Philistia (verse 12) were Israel's neighbors on the east and west. The phrase ‘the foes of Rezin’ in verse 11 is puzzling, since Rezin of Damascus was Israel's ally in 734 BC; most interpreters take it to mean Assyria, which destroyed Damascus and then turned on Israel, and some scholars emend the text to read ‘his foes’. Ashlar masonry, the ‘finished stone’ of verse 10, has been excavated in the royal quarter of Samaria from the ninth and eighth centuries BC, the kind of building the boast has in mind.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East a king's accession was accompanied by throne names and titles. Egyptian pharaohs received a fivefold royal titulary at their coronation, a set of formal names announcing what the reign would be, and Assyrian kings used long strings of epithets (great king, mighty king, king of the world). Some scholars, following Gerhard von Rad and Albrecht Alt, have suggested that the four names of verse 6 reflect a similar Judean practice, announced at a royal birth or enthronement. Psalm 2:7 (“You are My Son; today I have become Your Father”) shows that Judah spoke of the king as God's son on the day of his coronation. Even so, the titles of verse 6 go beyond anything claimed for a king of Judah. Mighty God (El Gibbor) is used of the Lord himself in 10:21, and Everlasting Father describes a king whose fatherly care for his people lasts forever.

The language of verse 4 comes from forced labor and slavery. A yoke was the wooden bar laid across the neck of an ox, and in the ancient Near East it also pictured the rule of a conqueror; Assyrian kings describe subject peoples as bearing the yoke of their lordship. The bar across the shoulders and the rod of the oppressor recall the taskmasters of Egypt (the same word, noges, in Exodus 3:7 and 5:6). The trampling boot of verse 5 uses a rare word generally explained as a borrowing from Akkadian, perhaps suggesting the heavy footwear of the Assyrian army; Assyrian palace reliefs show soldiers in laced boots. Burning boots and blood-soaked garments pictures the end of war: soldiers' gear is gathered and burned because it will never be needed again.

In the judgment poem the images come from ordinary life. Bricks of sun-dried mud and sycamore-fig beams were the cheap building materials of villages; dressed stone and imported cedar were the materials of palaces and temples, and 1 Kings 10:27 measures Solomon's wealth by saying cedar became as common as sycamore. The boast of verse 10 is to rebuild grander, not to repent. The palm branch and the reed (verse 14) are the high frond of a palm and the lowly marsh rush, a pair meaning everyone from top to bottom. Widows and orphans (verse 17) were the classic examples of the vulnerable whom Israel's law placed under God's special protection (Exodus 22:22-24, Deuteronomy 10:18). Right and left (verse 20) means in every direction.
literary:
The chapter has two very different parts. Verses 1 to 7 are a royal oracle of salvation, moving from darkness to light, from oppression to joy, and from war to peace. The verbs are mostly Hebrew perfects, which in prophecy often present what God will do as already settled. After the opening scene (verses 1 and 2) and the call to rejoice (verse 3), three reasons follow, each introduced by ‘for’: the yoke is broken (verse 4), the gear of war is burned (verse 5), and a child is born (verse 6). The birth is the climax and the ground of the rest. The poem is carefully linked: the yoke on the people's shoulder in verse 4 is replaced by the government on the child's shoulder in verse 6, and the oppressor's rod gives way to a reign of justice and righteousness. Verse 7 ends with a guarantee, “The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this”, a line repeated word for word in 37:32 about the survival of a remnant from Jerusalem.

Verses 8 to 21 are a judgment poem in three stanzas (8 to 12, 13 to 17, 18 to 21), each ending with the refrain “Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.” A fourth stanza follows in 10:1-4, and the same refrain appears in 5:25, so many scholars think the poem once stood with chapter 5 and was split when the material of 6:1 to 9:7 was placed between its parts. The stanzas move from outside enemies (Aram and Philistia) to the failure of leaders (the head and the tail) to the fire of wickedness itself consuming the society from within. The refrain shows judgment as a series of warnings, each unheeded. The contrast between the halves is deliberate: Israel's human kings and guides lead to ruin, while the promised king brings peace without end. In the Hebrew Bible the chapter division falls differently, so that the oracle of light begins in 8:23 and the whole chapter is numbered one verse lower (see the note on the text).

outline.t: Light for the lands in darkness
Joy, the broken yoke, and the end of war
Unto us a child is born
Israel's pride and the first judgment
Leaders cut off, head and tail

doctrines.note: The child of verses 6 and 7 is the clearest picture so far of the coming king: born into David's line, bearing titles that belong to God, reigning with justice and righteousness forever. Whatever its first occasion, the promise refuses to fit any king of Judah, and Christians confess this child as Jesus.

A child is born and a son is given: the pair joins a real human birth with a gift from God, and the child is called Mighty God, the LORD's own title in 10:21. Christian interpreters have long heard in the verse the one who is truly born of a human mother and truly the Son sent from the Father (Galatians 4:4).

The promised kingdom grows without end and rests on justice and righteousness, not conquest; it ends oppression and burns the equipment of war. It is established by the zeal of the LORD of Hosts, not by human effort or alliances.

The second stanza names the root failure: “the people did not return to Him who struck them; they did not seek the LORD of Hosts” (verse 13). Each blow was meant to turn Israel home, and repentance is presented as turning back to a person, not merely changing behavior.

The poem of verses 8 to 21 shows judgment answering persistent refusal to repent. Judgment comes from outside enemies, from the removal of leaders, and finally from the self-consuming fire of wickedness itself, and each time the people refuse, the hand stays raised.

words.note: Pele, wonder, part of the title Wonderful Counselor (pele yoets, literally ‘a wonder of a counselor’). The noun occurs about thirteen times, seven of them in the Psalms, and almost always of God's own extraordinary acts: the God “majestic in holiness, revered with praises, performing wonders” (Exodus 15:11), the wonders of old remembered in Psalm 77:11 and 14. Isaiah uses the related verb of the LORD himself in 28:29, “wonderful in counsel”. The child's counsel will be of the kind only God gives, in contrast to Ahaz's disastrous political counsel in chapter 7 and to the mediums of 8:19.

El, God, in the title El Gibbor, Mighty God. El occurs about 240 times in the Hebrew Bible, most often in poetry (Psalms and Job), usually of the true God and sometimes of gods in general. Paired with gibbor, mighty or warrior, it names the LORD in Deuteronomy 10:17 and Jeremiah 32:18, and the identical phrase in Isaiah 10:21 says a remnant will return “to the Mighty God”, which can only mean the LORD. Some interpreters render the title ‘godlike hero’ or ‘mighty warrior’, pointing to Ezekiel 32:21, where a plural form of the phrase describes human warriors, but within Isaiah the natural reading is Mighty God, marking this child as more than an ordinary king.

Av, father, one of the most common nouns in the Bible (about 1,200 times), here in Avi-ad, ‘father of perpetuity’, Everlasting Father. A king could be called a father to his people (Isaiah 22:21 says Eliakim will be a father to Jerusalem), and God is called Israel's father (Isaiah 63:16, 64:8). The title does not confuse the Son with the Father of later Trinitarian language; it describes the child's rule as fatherly care for his people that never ends, using ad, ‘forever’, a word most at home with God.

Shalom, peace, about 240 times, twenty-nine of them in Isaiah. It appears twice here: in the title Prince of Peace (sar shalom) and in the endless increase of peace (verse 7). Shalom means more than the absence of war. The standard lexicons give a range from completeness and soundness to welfare, health, prosperity, and harmony between persons and with God. The peace this king brings is wholeness restored in every direction, which is why his reign begins with the burning of the gear of war (verse 5).

Misrah, government or dominion, a rare noun found only in verses 6 and 7 of this chapter. It probably comes from a root meaning to rule, related to sar, prince or official. The government rests on the child's shoulder, the place where the yoke of oppression lay in verse 4, and of its increase there is no end. Justin Martyr (First Apology 35) read the government on his shoulder as a picture of the cross, which Jesus bore on his shoulders.

Qinah, zeal or jealousy, about forty-three times. It can describe destructive human envy (Proverbs 14:30) or rivalry (Ecclesiastes 4:4), a husband's jealousy (Numbers 5:14), and the burning commitment of God to his people and his name (Ezekiel 39:25, Zechariah 1:14). In verse 7 the zeal of the LORD of Hosts is the guarantee of the promise: God's passionate, exclusive devotion to what is his will accomplish what no king of Judah could.

Shuv, to turn or return, one of the commonest verbs in the Old Testament (over a thousand times). It is used for physical return, for God's anger turning away, and above all for repentance, turning back to God. The chapter uses it twice in a painful pairing: God's anger has not turned back (the refrain of verses 12, 17, and 21), because the people did not turn back to him (verse 13). The same verb lies behind the name Shear-jashub, ‘a remnant will return’ (7:3), and Isaiah 10:21 promises that a remnant will return to the Mighty God.

Or, light, about 120 times, twenty-seven of them in Isaiah, more than any book but Job. From the first day of creation (Genesis 1:3) light stands for life and God's saving presence, and darkness for chaos, death, and judgment. In verse 2 a great light dawns on those who walk in darkness; the same image returns when the Servant is made a light for the nations (42:6, 49:6) and when the glory of the LORD rises on Zion (60:1-3). The light comes to the people; they do not produce it.

christ:
Matthew 4:12-17 quotes verses 1 and 2 when Jesus, after John the Baptist's arrest, leaves Nazareth and settles in Capernaum by the sea, in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali. Matthew sees in this move the fulfillment of the great light dawning in Galilee of the nations: “the people living in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned” (Matthew 4:16). The point is geographical as well as theological. The region that first fell to Assyria, and that Jerusalem's leaders later despised (John 7:52), is where the Messiah's light first shines, and the verse's own phrase, Galilee of the nations, foreshadows his mission to the Gentiles. Luke 1:79 applies the same image to the coming of the Messiah whose way John prepares.

The child of verses 6 and 7 has been read throughout Christian history as Jesus. Gabriel's announcement to Mary gathers the elements of verse 7: “He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will never end!” (Luke 1:32-33). The pairing of a child born and a son given matches the New Testament's twofold confession of Jesus as truly born of a woman and truly sent from the Father (Galatians 4:4, John 3:16). The four names describe what Christians confess of him. He is the Wonderful Counselor, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). He is Mighty God, the LORD's own title in Isaiah 10:21, which is why the church has read this verse as one of the Old Testament's clearest witnesses to the deity of the Messiah. He is Everlasting Father, not by confusion with the Father but as the one whose care for his people never ends. He is the Prince of Peace, who is himself our peace (Ephesians 2:14) and who made peace through the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20).

The broken yoke of verse 4 finds its answer in Jesus' invitation to take his easy yoke (Matthew 11:28-30), and the burning of the gear of war anticipates the peace he announces and the kingdom that grows without end. The judgment poem that follows is part of the same picture: the refusal to return that brought ruin on Israel is what the Messiah's call to repentance, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 4:17), addresses in the very passage where Matthew quotes this chapter.
interpretation:
Jewish tradition has read the child in two main ways. The Aramaic Targum of Isaiah names him the Messiah, in whose days peace will increase, while treating the first titles as names of God who calls him. The Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 94a) reads the verse of Hezekiah, counting eight names for him, and explains the unusual closed letter mem in the first word of verse 7 with a tradition attributed to Bar Kappara: God wished to make Hezekiah the Messiah and Sennacherib Gog and Magog, but the purpose was closed off because Hezekiah did not sing God's praise after his deliverance. Rashi followed the Targum's division, taking Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, and Everlasting Father as names of God who called the child Prince of Peace, and identified the child as Hezekiah; Abraham Ibn Ezra, also reading of Hezekiah, gave all the names to the child.

Christian reading began with the Gospels. Justin Martyr (First Apology 35, around 155) quoted the verse and took the government on his shoulder as a sign of the cross. The Septuagint had not given the four titles but read ‘his name is called Messenger of great counsel’, and that phrase, in Latin magni consilii Angelus, became the words of the introit for the Christmas Day Mass, Puer natus est nobis, which Thomas Tallis used as the basis of his Mass of 1554. Jerome's Latin restored the titles and counted six names. Calvin's commentary on Isaiah argued at length against the Jewish readings that Mighty God must be read of the child.

In modern critical scholarship Gerhard von Rad (in a 1947 essay on the Judean royal ritual) and Albrecht Alt (in a 1950 essay on 8:23 to 9:6) compared the names with the throne names announced at an Egyptian pharaoh's accession and read the poem as an accession oracle for a Judean king, Hezekiah or a hoped-for successor. Many critical scholars date it to Isaiah's own lifetime; others place it later, in the time of Josiah. Evangelical commentators such as John Oswalt (The Book of Isaiah, Chapters 1-39, 1986) and J. Alec Motyer (The Prophecy of Isaiah, 1993) read it as a direct prophecy of the divine Messiah. Modern Jewish translations follow the medieval reading and render the names as a sentence about God.

In worship the passage belongs to Christmas and Epiphany. The Revised Common Lectionary appoints verses 2 to 7 for Christmas Eve or Day (Proper I) in all three years, and verses 1 to 4 with Matthew 4:12-23 on the Third Sunday after the Epiphany in Year A. At King's College, Cambridge, whose Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols has been broadcast since 1928, verses 2 and 6 to 7 are the third lesson. Handel's Messiah (1742) sets verse 2 as the bass aria that follows the prophecies of Part One and verse 6 as the chorus ‘For unto us a child is born’, whose running music Handel reworked from an Italian duet he had written in July 1741, No, di voi non vo' fidarmi.
text:
Verse numbering differs between Hebrew and English Bibles. Hebrew Bibles place the first verse of the English chapter at the end of chapter 8, as 8:23, so that English 9:2 to 9:21 are Hebrew 9:1 to 9:20; commentaries that follow the Hebrew therefore discuss ‘Isaiah 9:5’ where English readers have the four names in 9:6. The Latin Vulgate follows the Hebrew division.

Several lines read differently in the ancient versions and English Bibles. In verse 1 the two verbs can be read as a contrast (in the past he humbled, in the future he will honor), as in the BSB and most modern versions, or as two blows, a lighter and then a heavier affliction, as in the KJV. In verse 3 the written Hebrew (ketiv) has lo with an aleph, ‘not’, giving ‘you have not increased the joy’, which the KJV translated; the Masoretic marginal reading (qere) has lo with a waw, ‘to it’, giving ‘increased its joy’, which nearly all modern versions follow. In verse 6 the Septuagint lacks the four titles and reads ‘Messenger of great counsel’, while later Greek revisions and the Vulgate give the full list; the 1917 Jewish Publication Society version transliterates the whole as one name, and later Jewish translations render it as a sentence about God. In verse 7 the Masoretic Text writes the first word with a closed final mem in the middle of a word, a unique scribal feature discussed above. In verse 11 ‘the foes of Rezin’ is often emended to ‘his foes’. In verse 20 the Hebrew reads ‘the flesh of his own arm’ (KJV, ESV); the BSB's ‘his own offspring’ follows a slight change of vowels, and the RSV's ‘his neighbor’ follows another proposed correction. Matthew's quotation of verses 1 and 2 follows neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint exactly.

teach.big: God answers the darkness his people have brought on themselves not with a better strategy but with a child, the Mighty God born in David's line, whose reign of justice and peace will never end, while those who refuse to return to him are consumed by the pride that rejects him.

outline.t: The light comes first to the places that suffered first; God's rescue begins where the darkness was deepest, and the people receive light they could not produce.
God's reign brings joy like harvest and victory, breaks oppression as he did for Gideon, and ends war itself by burning its equipment.
The ground of all this is a child: born and given, carrying the government on his shoulders, named with titles that belong to God, reigning in justice forever by the LORD's own zeal.
Pride answers disaster by promising to build bigger instead of turning back, and God's hand stays raised.
The root failure is refusing to return to God, and leaders who tell comfortable lies swallow up those who follow them.
Wickedness is its own fire: a society that rejects God consumes itself, brother against brother, until it turns on its neighbors.

teach.pitfalls:
The first pitfall is to preach verses 6 and 7 as if they stood alone, cut off from the darkness of chapter 8 and the judgment of verses 8 to 21. The promise is bright because the night around it is real; without the refrain of God's raised hand the child becomes a seasonal ornament rather than God's answer to a society destroying itself. The second is to read the four names as a list of what Jesus will be for me personally (my counselor, my father), which is true as far as it goes but misses that the titles are royal and public: they describe a king whose government, justice, and peace reach a whole world.

A third pitfall is to handle Everlasting Father carelessly. The title does not mean that the Son is the Father, an error the early church rejected (modalism); it describes a king whose care for his people is fatherly and endless. A fourth is to overstate the argument from Mighty God. The title is strong evidence, especially alongside 10:21, but Jewish and critical readers have serious reasons for their views, and teachers should present them fairly rather than suggest the verse settles every question by itself. Finally, avoid applying the judgment stanzas to other people's nations or churches while exempting one's own. The poem addresses God's own people, and the prophets' sharpest words fall on those who claim him.
teach.pastoral: The opening verses speak to anyone living in the shadow of death: the grieving, the depressed, those whose region or family has been hit first and hardest. Teach that the light comes to people who can do nothing but see it, without implying that those still in darkness lack faith. The judgment stanzas, especially verse 17, can trouble tender consciences and those who have been widowed or orphaned; explain that the verse measures how completely a society had rotted, not a change in God's care for the vulnerable, which the law and the prophets affirm everywhere. Verses 15 and 16 speak to people harmed by leaders who misled them; they may take comfort that God holds such leaders accountable.

hard.q: Were the titles in verse 6 meant for a human king of Isaiah's day, or for a divine Messiah?
hard.a:
The strongest case for a human king is historical and grammatical. The poem uses the language of royal birth and accession familiar from the ancient Near East, where kings received throne names at coronation; Gerhard von Rad and Albrecht Alt read it as an accession oracle for a Judean king. Jewish tradition from the Talmud (Sanhedrin 94a) to Rashi and Ibn Ezra identified the child with Hezekiah, the faithful son of faithless Ahaz, whose deliverance from Sennacherib in 701 BC answered the darkness of the Assyrian crisis. On the grammar, the verb ‘he called’ has no stated subject, and the Targum and Rashi divide the words so that Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, and Everlasting Father describe God, who names the child Prince of Peace; modern Jewish translations render the whole as a sentence about God, much as Isaiah's own children bore sentence-names. Those who give all the titles to the child can still argue, as some critical scholars do, that Mighty God means ‘godlike hero’ (compare the plural phrase for warriors in Ezekiel 32:21) and that royal language in the ancient world was often extravagant; Psalm 45:6 even addresses the king as God.

Christian interpreters respond on several fronts. The identical phrase El Gibbor appears in 10:21 of the LORD himself, only a chapter later, and in Deuteronomy 10:17 and Jeremiah 32:18 for God. The titles are given to the child in the natural reading of the sentence, as the Septuagint's later revisions, the Vulgate, and Ibn Ezra all took them. The reign described has no end and its peace no limit, and no historical king of Judah, Hezekiah included, fulfilled that; Hezekiah's own reign ended with the prophecy of exile to Babylon (39:5-7). Commentators such as John Oswalt and J. Alec Motyer conclude that the child is the divine Messiah. Others take a middle path: the oracle may have been spoken for the royal hope of Isaiah's day, but its language deliberately outruns any son of David then living, so that the hope remained open until the New Testament found it realized in Jesus (Luke 1:32-33). The church's confession that Jesus is God does not rest on this verse alone, but Christians have long read it as one of the clearest Old Testament witnesses to that confession, while Jewish readers continue to hear in it the praise of the God who delivered Hezekiah.

hard.q: How can the God who defends widows and orphans say he has no compassion on them (verse 17)?
hard.a:
The objection is moral and sharp. The law commands care for the fatherless and the widow and says God himself defends them (Exodus 22:22-24, Deuteronomy 10:18), yet verse 17 says the Lord takes no pleasure in Israel's young men and has no compassion on its fatherless and widows. Readers troubled by the Old Testament's portraits of divine violence, such as Eric Seibert (Disturbing Divine Behavior, 2009), argue that such texts reflect the prophets' own culture and theology of retribution, and that Christians should not accept every portrayal of God's wrath at face value. Skeptics add that collective judgment, in which the vulnerable suffer with the guilty, seems unjust by any standard.

Responses begin with the verse itself, which gives its reason: “For every one of them is godless and wicked, and every mouth speaks folly.” The line measures how completely the corruption had spread; it does not say God hates the weak but that even those whom he normally protects had joined the profanity and lies of the leaders (verses 15 and 16). Abraham Joshua Heschel (The Prophets, 1962) argued that the wrath of God in the prophets is not a blind rage but an expression of his pathos, his wounded concern for his people and for justice, and that it is always tied to a call to return; this poem's refrain, ‘His hand is still upraised’, pictures judgment as repeated warning. Others note that the chapter describes judgment largely as God handing people over to what they have chosen: wickedness burns like fire (verse 18) and the society devours itself (verses 19 to 21), a pattern Paul traces in Romans 1:24-28. Miroslav Volf (Exclusion and Embrace, 1996) argued that belief in God's judgment of evil is what keeps victims from taking vengeance into their own hands. Christian readers also point out that the same God who speaks here promises in the same chapter a king whose reign rests on justice and righteousness, and that the prophets' laments over the suffering of the innocent in national judgment (Lamentations 2:11-12) show that Scripture does not treat that suffering lightly. How to hold together divine judgment and divine compassion remains a question on which thoughtful Christians and Jews continue to reflect.

observe: What three reasons for joy does the poem give, each beginning with ‘for’ (verses 4, 5, and 6)?
What are the four names of the child in verse 6, and what does verse 7 say about his reign?
What refrain closes verses 12, 17, and 21, and how does verse 13 explain why the refrain keeps returning?
interpret: Why do you think the light dawns first in Zebulun and Naphtali, the lands that suffered first under Assyria, and why does Matthew care about that?
How does the government on the child's shoulder (verse 6) answer the yoke on the people's shoulder (verse 4)?
What does the boast of verse 10 reveal about the difference between recovering from disaster and repenting?
apply: Which of the four names in verse 6 speaks most directly to what you need from God right now, and why?
Where are you tempted to answer loss by promising to rebuild bigger rather than by turning back to God?
Verses 15 and 16 warn about leaders who mislead. What guides do you follow, and how do you test what they tell you?
